method: POST (JSON body) for SearchSailingRoutes; GET for GetAllAvailableCountriesAndPorts
params:
GetAllAvailableCountriesAndPorts: plain GET, no params, no auth. Returns {Countries:[...], Ports:[580 x {PortId, LocationName, LocationCode, CountryName, CountryIsoCode, lat, lon}]}. 13 UK ports incl. PortId 361 SOUTHAMPTON/GBSOU, 365 FELIXSTOWE/GBFXT, 1375 LONDON GATEWAY PORT/GBLGP, 357 TILBURY/GBTIL, 362 LIVERPOOL/GBLIV, 557 TEESPORT/GBTEE, 669 IMMINGHAM/GBIMM, 821 PORTBURY/GBPRU (also BELFAST, GRANGEMOUTH, GREENOCK, SOUTH SHIELDS, THAMESPORT). No Grimsby or Sheerness in the dictionary.

SearchSailingRoutes body (minimum viable set, verified): {"FromDate":"2026-09-03","fromPortId":365,"toPortId":63}. The site also sends language:"en" and dataSourceId:"{E9CCBD25-6FBA-4C5C-85F6-FC4F9E5A931F}" but I verified both are OPTIONAL — dropping them returns byte-identical results. FromDate is mandatory (omitting it returns IsSuccess:false "Service is temporarily unavailable"). Returns roughly 8 weeks of sailings forward from FromDate; advancing FromDate walks the window forward.

CRITICAL HEADER: the POST endpoints require `x-requested-with: XMLHttpRequest`. Without it you get HTTP 200 with a body of literally `""` — a silent empty, not an error. This is deterministic, not flaky: I bisected it across header variants, 2 runs each. Also send a normal `accept` / `accept-encoding` / `user-agent`; node:https with a bare header set gets 403 from Akamai, with a normal set gets 200. No cookies, no token, no session warm-up, no prior page visit needed — every request in my tests was from a cold process with an empty cookie jar.

Crawl shape: 8 UK ports x ~570 non-GB destination ports = ~4,640 POSTs. Measured 150 requests at concurrency 4 in 22s with zero failures, so a full sweep is ~11 minutes. Trimming destinations to the countries the business actually ships to cuts that to a few hundred requests.
responseShape:
{"IsSuccess":true,"Data":[group],"ResultTimestamp":"Search schedule results provided by MSC on 03.09.2026 at ..."}

Each group has Key{MaritimeServiceName, PortOfLoading, PortOfDischarge, IsDirectRoute}, PortOfLoad / PortOfLoadUnCode / PortOfLoadId, PortOfDischarge / PortOfDischargeUnCode / PortOfDischargeId, RoutingType ("Direct" | "Transhipment"), and Routes[] — one entry per sailing.

Per sailing (group.Routes[i]):
- vessel name      -> VesselName
- voyage number    -> DepartureVoyageNo  (always published, e.g. "RP637R", "NY636A")
- UK load port     -> group.PortOfLoad + group.PortOfLoadUnCode (e.g. "SOUTHAMPTON" / "GBSOU"); also RouteScheduleLegDetails[0].DeparturePortName/DeparturePortUNCode plus DepartureEquipmentHandlingFacilityName (the actual terminal, e.g. "ROYAL SEAFORTH CONTAINER TERMINAL")
- destination port -> group.PortOfDischarge + PortOfDischargeUnCode
- destination country -> NOT in the route payload. Join PortOfDischargeId (or the UN/LOCODE prefix) against the Ports dictionary from GetAllAvailableCountriesAndPorts, which carries CountryName + CountryIsoCode. Verified this join resolves cleanly for every row I pulled.
- departure date   -> EstimatedDepartureDate (ISO, "2026-09-11T07:00:00") and EstimatedDepartureDateFormatted
- arrival date     -> EstimatedArrivalDate (ISO) and EstimatedArrivalDateFormatted
- bonus: TotalTransitTime ("30 days"), TotalTransitTimeHours, CO2FootPrint, CutOffs{ContainerYardCutOffDate, ReeferCutOffDate, DangerousCargoCutOffDate, ShippingInstructionsCutOffDate, VerifiedGrossMassCutOffDate}, and RouteScheduleLegDetails[] giving every transhipment leg with per-leg vessel {VesselName, VesselImoCode, VesselBuiltYear, VesselFlag}, voyage no, port and dates. The last leg is a terminator with only arrival fields populated.
ukLanes:
All 8 target UK ports in MSC's dictionary return live sailings: Southampton, Felixstowe, London Gateway, Tilbury, Liverpool, Teesport, Immingham, Portbury. MSC also lists Belfast, Grangemouth, Greenock, South Shields and Thamesport. Grimsby and Sheerness do not exist in MSC's port list at all.

Destinations confirmed reachable from UK ports in my probe: Nigeria (Tin Can/Lagos), South Africa (Durban), Kenya (Mombasa), Tanzania (Dar es Salaam), Ghana (Tema), USA (New York), Singapore, UAE (Jebel Ali), Fiji (Lautoka). Of the 150 destinations I swept from Felixstowe, 103 returned sailings and 47 returned a clean "no results available for the selected port pair" — so roughly two thirds of MSC's global port list is reachable from a single UK port, mostly via transhipment through Antwerp/Le Havre/Sines. Direct sailings are the minority (55 of 439 rows in the probe) but are flagged explicitly via RoutingType/IsDirectRoute, so you can filter.

Note the port-pair asymmetry is real, not noise: Southampton->Tin Can and Tilbury->Tin Can both legitimately return "no results" while Felixstowe, London Gateway, Liverpool, Teesport and Portbury to Tin Can all return sailings. Do not treat an empty pair as a fetch failure.
blockers:
Three things to build around. None of them is fatal, but the first is a real unknown I could not test from here.

1. AKAMAI BOT MANAGER IS IN FRONT OF THIS, AND IT FINGERPRINTS THE CLIENT. curl 8.18 gets 403 "Access Denied" on both the HTML page and the API even with identical headers and identical HTTP version — its Schannel TLS fingerprint is rejected outright. Node passes: both global fetch (undici) and node:https core return 200, provided you send a normal accept / accept-encoding / user-agent set (node:https with a bare header set gets 403). So plain Node is fine today, but I tested from a residential UK IP. I CANNOT verify from here whether Akamai will score a datacentre ASN differently, and Akamai commonly does. Before committing, do one smoke run from the actual cloud runner. If it 403s there, this flips to "no" and no amount of header tuning from a datacentre IP will reliably fix it.

2. THE SILENT-EMPTY FAILURE MODE. Omitting x-requested-with: XMLHttpRequest returns HTTP 200 with body `""` — not a 4xx, not an error object. Any health check that only asserts status===200 will pass while collecting nothing, which is exactly the shape of failure that would block your weekly run. Treat `""`, a non-JSON body, and a zero-row sweep as hard failures distinct from IsSuccess:false, which is a legitimate "this pair is not served".

3. DESTINATION COUNTRY REQUIRES A JOIN, AND THE CRAWL IS N x M. The route payload gives you the discharge port name and UN/LOCODE but no country, so you must fetch the port dictionary first and join on PortOfDischargeId. Fetch it every run and fail loudly if a discharge port id is missing from it, rather than emitting a row with a null country. And there is no "all destinations from port X" call — point-to-point requires both ends, so a full sweep is 8 UK ports x ~570 destinations = ~4,640 requests, about 11 minutes at concurrency 4. Trim the destination list to the countries the business actually ships to and this drops to a few hundred requests.

Lesser notes: this is an undocumented internal endpoint on a Sitecore site with a versioned asset bundle (?v=4100289), so it can change without warning — pin a canary port pair (Felixstowe->Durban is stable and cheap) and alert if its shape changes. Grimsby and Sheerness are not in MSC's port list at all. The response window is ~8 weeks forward from FromDate; advance FromDate to page further out.

evidence:
What I requested and what came back, all via plain Node with no packages:

1. GET https://www.msc.com/en/search-a-schedule
   - node fetch: 200, 280,336 bytes of server-rendered HTML. The API paths are in the markup as data- attributes on the Alpine component (data-api-search-sailing-routes="/api/feature/tools/SearchSailingRoutes" etc.), so no browser was needed to find them. I read the request payload shapes out of /_sc/Assets/scripts/main.js (200, 1,052,155 bytes).
   - curl 8.18 (Schannel), same URL, same UA: 403 Akamai "Access Denied". Noted below.

2. GET /api/feature/tools/GetAllAvailableCountriesAndPorts
   - node fetch, no headers at all beyond defaults: 200, 118,645 bytes JSON, 580 ports / 13 UK.

3. POST /api/feature/tools/SearchSailingRoutes
   - node fetch with x-requested-with: 200 with full route data. Liverpool->New York 6,425 bytes; Felixstowe->Tin Can 166,646 bytes; Southampton->Mombasa 41,887 bytes.
   - Same request WITHOUT x-requested-with: 200 with body `""`. Bisected across 5 header variants x 2 runs: only the x-requested-with variant returned data, all others returned `""` consistently.
   - GET with the params as a query string: 500 (HTML error page). It is POST-only in production.
   - Missing FromDate: 200 with IsSuccess:false "Service is temporarily unavailable".
   - Unserved pair: 200 with IsSuccess:false "There are currently no results available for the selected port pair." Clean, distinguishable from an error.

4. Load test: 40 sequential requests in 24.4s, 0 errors. 150 requests at concurrency 4 in 22.0s, 0 errors, 0 empty bodies, 0 non-200s. No rate limiting or throttling observed.

5. POST /api/feature/tools/SearchArrivalsDepartures {"language":"en","PortMscCode":"GBSOU"} also works (200, 4,093 bytes, real data: YM TROPHY voy 022W, MSC ELKE F voy RP635R with cut-off dates). But I am NOT recommending it: it is a live 3-day port window and it has no destination port, no destination country and no arrival date. It fails the requirement. SearchSailingRoutes is the one to use.

6. Downloadable timetables: none. I fetched /en/local-information/europe/united-kingdom (200, 285,845 bytes), /en/sailing-schedules and /en/our-routes and scraped every .pdf/.xlsx/.xls href. The only documents on the UK page are gender pay gap statements and a tax strategy. MSC publishes no public PDF or Excel timetable, so option 1 from your list is genuinely unavailable and the JSON API is the route.
